Find how material removal and breaking really work, aiming at ONE simple unifying law for a game:

- impulse vs energy: blunt vs sharp tools (pressure = force / contact area; a sharp edge concentrates it), why a knife cuts leather but bounces off stone, why a hammer shatters glass but dents iron.

# Task 61 / physics: how material removal and breaking really work, and ONE simple law for the game

Status legend: [S] = number from a cited source, [E] = my estimate or derived value (marked), [K] = standard textbook knowledge I did not re-verify in this session.

## 0. The answer in six lines (read this first)

1. Real breaking always costs energy in only TWO ways: (a) **volume price P** (J per cm3): squashing, shearing, bending, dragging stuff out of the way; (b) **surface price R** (J per m2): making a new crack/cut surface. Everything else (heat, noise, flying chips) is loss.
2. Which term wins depends on one length: **l = R / P** (metres). Glass: 8 nm. Granite: 0.7 um. Wood across grain: 0.4 mm. Rubber: 0.5 mm. Steel: 0.09 mm. Small l = brittle (cracks, chips, shatters). Big l = tough/fibrous (dents, bends, tears, cuts).
3. A blow cannot bite unless **pressure = force / contact area** reaches the material's **hardness H (about 3 x strength, Tabor)**. Sharp edge = tiny area = big pressure. A tool must be harder than what it cuts, otherwise the tool is what gets damaged.
4. Once it bites, the dent/crush volume is simply **V = E / H** (energy / hardness); a crack grows only if the blow still has energy for

The numbers are standard handbook and literature values from memory, and I marked each estimate with (E). Verify them before shipping. Main finding: the energy to remove 1 cm3 is about 2-5 times the material's strength in MPa (1 MPa = 1 J/cm3). Granite is about 200 MPa and 750 J/cm3, which is x3.75. Steel machining is about 3500 J/cm3. So ONE strength number per material gives the cost of carving a volume, and ONE toughness number (K or tear energy) gives the cost of a crack or cut per area. Density gives the mass. The rest is a class flag. Proposed classes: brittle, grained-fibrous (wood), fibrous-soft, ductile (metals), granular (sand, soil, snow), plastic-wet (clay, mud), soft-tough (leather, rubber, flesh), liquid, thermoplastic or wax-resin (softens with heat), composite-layered. You work on POLUS, a Godot 4.7 first-person survival sandbox (browser build: WebGL2 Compatibility renderer, no threads, Jolt physics, server-authoritative multiplayer that sends inputs/events and every peer computes the same result). Project root: polus (relative paths are relative to it). Long-term vision: survive, die, reincarnate into an NPC of your settlement; epochs from stone age to space. Today the game has an axe/pick/shovel/hammer/hands with materials and body strength (one swing-energy formula), and three material models: wood (5 mm slices x 3-7 mm cell bitmaps for accounting + CSG picture; coarse 24x24 fibre mask for strength), stone (exact triangle mesh, crush 750 J/cm3 for granite, crack costs G_eff x area with 10% of the energy and needs a free face, flake on a 9x15 heightfield), soil (heightmap 12.5 cm nodes, integer mm, repose 36 deg). Pieces < 10 kg are bag items. The full verified description: .orchestra/tasks/60/notes.md and the checker report summary there; also .orchestra/tasks/57/numbers/formulas.md.

The designer (Maxim, not a programmer) asked (translated): "Google how all this works in real physics, and let's bring everything to ONE simple formula, no complications, optimised purely for the game so it plays interesting and fun. Maybe something simple on invisible voxels, or no voxels and just pure physics formulas. Give me several interesting, understandable variants, as pretty as now with diagrams. And think what other materials can be in the game: leather, cloth, water, iron, plastic, glass - what else exists in the world."

Rules: READ ONLY for the project except your own notes folder named below (write your notes and raw data there). Never write outside the project folder. Do not run Godot, builds or servers. Use WebSearch / WebFetch for real sources; cite URLs. Prefer real measured numbers with a source; mark estimates as estimates. Plain English in notes; fields ending in _ru must be in simple Russian a non-programmer reads in one go (no jargon, or jargon explained). Your final answer = the structured result.

YOUR PART: HOW GAMES DO IT (notes: .orchestra/tasks/61/games/notes.md).
For each, how materials and destruction work inside, what the player experiences, what is fun, what costs (performance, network), what failed: Teardown (voxels, material types, structural integrity), Noita (falling-sand pixel simulation, every pixel a material), The Powder Toy, Dwarf Fortress (material properties: shear/impact yield, fracture, strain at yield; weapon vs armor layer combat), Zelda Breath of the Wild / Tears of the Kingdom 'chemistry engine' (simple material tags and rules: fire, water, electricity, wind), Minecraft (block hardness x tool tier table), Valheim (structural integrity of building materials), Space Engineers / Medieval Engineers (voxel terrain + block deformation), Red Faction Guerrilla (stress-based building collapse), Instruments of Destruction, BeamNG (soft-body node-beam), Besiege, From the Depths, Kenshi / Exanima / Mordhau / Kingdom Come (damage vs armor materials), Astroneer / Deep Rock Galactic (terrain digging), Rust / Ark (material tiers), Hydroneer, 7 Days to Die (block structural integrity + material hp), Enshrouded, Abiotic Factor, Tiny Glade, any physics sandbox with materials you find (People Playground: materials, sharpness, temperature!), Garry's Mod material surface props.
Focus: which systems make ONE rule work for many materials; invisible voxels vs mesh vs particles vs tables; multiplayer determinism (Teardown multiplayer, 7DTD); what players love. Sources with URLs (GDC talks, devlogs, wikis).

Bottom line: every game that handles many materials keeps ONE unchanging rule and puts the differences into a per-material table (Minecraft, DF, Rust, Valheim, 7DTD, GMod, Powder Toy). The two most useful physical models are DF's energy vs material strength and BeamNG's \"when it bends / when it breaks\" pair. For multiplayer, the only approach that shipped is Teardown's: send small deterministic cut commands built on integer math, never voxel data. Limits: the DF wiki, Fandom, GDC Vault and Kenshi pages returned 429/402/403, so some numbers come from search summaries. I found no sourced Mordhau or Kenshi data. The BeamNG whitepaper PDF was unreadable.", "findings": [{"title": "Teardown: voxels, 7 material types, deterministic command stream", "detail": "World = thousands of small ~10 cm voxel volumes, each with its own grid and free to move or rotate. Each voxel points into a material palette (wood, metal, glass, plastic, masonry, foliage, dirt). A hit just deletes voxels, and a split creates new bodies. Structural integrity was left out on purpose (a house stands on one voxel). Multiplayer: sending voxel data 'completely choked the connection'; a mod that synced inputs drifted out of sync. What worked: destruction rewritten in fixed-point integers, the server sends 'cut this shape at x,y,z' commands on a reliable ordered stream, size independent of object size. Late join replays the command log (a full scene is 30-50 MB), and the log is capped, after which join-in-progress is disabled. Merging took about 3 months. This matches POLUS's 'send events, everyone computes the same' design.", "numbers": "~10 cm voxel; 7 materials; ~1 Mbit/client; 12 players; scene 30-50 MB", "source": "https://blog.voxagon.se/2026/03/13/teardown-multiplayer.html ; https://80.lv/articles/teardown-developer-breaks-down-multiplayer-and-voxel-destruction-tech ; https://playqub.it/blog/teardown-voxel-destruction/"}, {"title": "Noita and Powder Toy: one cell = one material, a few rules", "detail": "Most fun per rule of any system, but 2D only. Low strain at yield means it shatters. Only impact strain at yield is verified to matter, so most of the numbers are decoration (the failure). # Task 61 design notes: one material law, 5 variants

Inputs: physics/notes.md, games/notes.md, catalog/materials.md (task 61), 57/numbers/formulas.md, code headers
(world/items/matter.gd, world/tools/impact.gd, tools.gd, chop/wood_cuts.gd, rocks/spall.gd, dig/dig_layer.gd).

## Core law (all variants rest on it)
E_blow x eta = P*V + R*A, bite only if F/S >= H (tool must also be harder than H, else it dulls/bends).
P = J/cm3 to crush/remove (approx 2-5 x strength MPa; POLUS today: pine 10, oak 27.5, granite 750, loam 0.04).
R = J/cm2 of new crack or cut face (glass 0.0008, granite 0.011, pine along 0.016 / across 0.18, leather ~1 [E], steel ~10).
Brittleness length l = R/P: tiny -> cracks and shatters; large -> dents, tears, bends.
Today's code is already this law in 3 disguises:
- wood: V = ETA E/(KAPPA sigma) -> P = 5 sigma_perp; chip split along grain = cheap R.
- stone: crush V = 0.8 E_eff/H (P = 750 J/cm3 granite) + crack G_eff*A with 10 % of E (R = 3K^2/E = 112 J/m2).
- soil: V = dig_eff E / 40 kJ/m3 (P = 0.04 J/cm3, R = 0), plus repose relaxation.

## Variants
A Price list (pure formulas, today's meshes) | B invisible voxels 2 cm | C bonds/springs |
D classes + tags | E hybrid "one formula, a canvas per class" (RECOMMENDED).
